content: Non-specific cough in children is defined as a non-productive cough that occurs without any identifiable respiratory disease or known cause. In such cases, there is often speculation that asthma might be the underlying condition, a concept referred to as cough variant asthma. Advocates of this theory suggest trying asthma medications, including inhaled corticosteroids, as a potential treatment. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of inhaled corticosteroids in treating non-specific cough in children older than two years. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted in databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, with the search being up-to-date as of March 2004. The inclusion criteria for the study required randomized or quasi-randomized controlled clinical trials where inhaled corticosteroids, such as beclomethasone dipropionate (BDP), fluticasone propionate (FP), triamcinolone acetonide (TAA), or other corticosteroids, were administered to children over the age of two for the treatment of cough. Two independent reviewers assessed the articles for inclusion and evaluated their methodological quality. Data from the selected trials were extracted by both reviewers and analyzed using the Cochrane Collaboration's RevMan software. Ultimately, two trials met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 123 participants. One trial compared inhaled beclomethasone dipropionate (400 micrograms per day) with a placebo, while the other compared fluticasone propionate (2 mg per day for three days, followed by 1 mg per day for 11 days) with a placebo. Both studies utilized metered-dose inhalers with spacers for drug delivery. The results showed that at a lower dose of inhaled corticosteroids, there was no significant difference in cough reduction between the beclomethasone and placebo groups. However, at a higher dose, there was a notable improvement in the frequency of nocturnal cough after two weeks in children with persistent nocturnal cough. Despite this, a smaller but still significant improvement was also observed in the placebo group. The authors concluded that in one study, beclomethasone dipropionate at a dose of 400 micrograms per day was no more effective than a placebo in reducing cough frequency, whether measured objectively or subjectively. While there may be a slight improvement with very high doses of inhaled corticosteroids, the clinical significance of this improvement is unlikely to be meaningful or beneficial.
